endorsements.quote: Patient-facing XAI interfaces should prioritise health literacy, using clear visualisations and avoiding technical jargon while maintaining accuracy.
Respiratory journals should encourage transparent reporting of AI methodologies, including explanation approaches, in published research.
Clinicians must also learn to identify misleading explanations, recognise data bias, and evaluate model generalisability.

Continuing medical education programmes should incorporate XAI modules tailored to respiratory medicine, enabling established practitioners to develop digital literacy and critical evaluation skills [ 19 ].

unlisted_practices: Develop standardised metrics to assess the reliability and clinical utility of XAI tools in respiratory medicine.
Strengthen interdisciplinary collaboration among clinicians, developers, and regulators so AI innovations remain clinically relevant and patient-centred.
Design policy frameworks and funding strategies that support integration of transparent AI tools and prevent opaque proprietary solutions from dominating.
Professional societies should establish best-practice guidelines for XAI implementation and curate validated XAI tools.
Regulators should provide clear guidance on what constitutes adequate AI explanation and how explanation quality should be validated.
Validate AI explanations against expert interpretation and ensure they are clinically meaningful rather than merely technical.
Weigh interpretability against accuracy case by case, prioritising interpretability in high-stakes decisions.

screen.reason: This is a Viewpoint commentary discussing explainable AI (XAI) frameworks, deployment considerations, governance, and clinical integration in respiratory medicine.
